medley

/MED-lee/ — rhymes with deadly · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A medley is a mix of different things combined into one, such as a piece of music made up of parts from several songs.

The band closed with a medley of songs from their first album.

Example

The orchestra performed a medley of pieces from different composers, arranged so that each movement flowed naturally into the next.

Medley precisely names the deliberate blending of distinct pieces into one artistic whole. A simpler word like 'mixture' would miss the sense that these different pieces were intentionally combined for a unified effect.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

collection: A collection is a group of things gathered together — stamps, shells, songs — with nothing said about how they relate to one another. A medley goes further: its different pieces are deliberately blended into one continuous whole, each part flowing into the next.

assortment: An assortment is a mixed selection of various kinds, a spread you choose from — assorted chocolates in a box. A medley is not for choosing from: its varied pieces are joined and performed as one, moving together as a single work.

compilation: A compilation gathers finished songs or writings side by side, each kept whole and separate — a greatest-hits album, an anthology. A medley stitches pieces of different works into one continuous performance, so the joins themselves become part of the art.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

uniformity: sameness, with no variety at all

monotony: dull sameness repeated without change

Where it sits · how smoothly varied pieces flow together

combination → mixture → arrangement → medley

combination vs. medley: Combination is the most general word on this scale: a combination just puts things together, while a medley weaves many different pieces into one flowing whole.

mixture vs. medley: Mixture is broader and plainer than medley; a mixture blends things of any kind, while a medley specifically strings varied pieces — often songs — into a single performance.

arrangement vs. medley: Arrangement is close to medley but less colorful: an arrangement orders its pieces carefully, while a medley delights in jumping between many different sources inside one seamless sequence.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mesler: to mix (Old French)

Put it together: Medley reached English in one piece from Old French mesler, 'to mix,' which traces back to Latin miscere - the same mixing root behind mix and miscellaneous. A medley is things mixed into one whole, like several songs blended into a single performance. There is no prefix or suffix to peel off here; the whole word does the mixing.

Use the root in a new word: meddle: Aunt Rosa cannot resist the urge to meddle whenever her sisters plan a party.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / slightly formal

Medley works best when describing the deliberate combination of distinct pieces—especially in music or art—that blend together as one cohesive work. For items simply grouped together or randomly mixed, use 'collection,' 'mixture,' or 'assortment' instead.
